claims.text: Thermally activated diffusion causes Mg segregation in non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys.
Mg segregation promotes formation of a protective Mg-rich oxide layer at high temperature.
Uneven Mg distribution establishes localized galvanic cells that accelerate ambient aqueous corrosion.
The initial alloy has a homogeneous elemental distribution in a disordered solid solution.
The initial alloy contains dispersed metastable intermetallic precursor phases.
Rapid solidification produces the required non-equilibrium state.
The proposed alloy has a density below 6 g/cm3.
The treated alloy is subjected to controlled oxidation at 600–800°C and then compared with an untreated control in ambient aqueous corrosion testing.
Thermal treatment forms Mg-rich oxide precipitates along grain boundaries.
Thermal treatment forms Mg-rich oxide precipitates within former intermetallic regions.
Elevated temperature accelerates Mg diffusion toward grain boundaries.
Segregated Mg forms a continuous, adherent Mg-rich oxide scale.
The continuous Mg-rich oxide scale improves high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the as-cast state.
Thermal exposure increases localized aqueous corrosion, including pitting, relative to the as-cast state.
The as-cast baseline lacks significant grain-boundary segregation and stable oxide scales.
The proposed behavior occurs only in rapidly solidified alloys.
The proposed behavior requires Mg content above a critical concentration.
Changes in composition or processing may alter the transformation kinetics.
The Mg-segregation kinetics, critical Mg concentration, and reproducibility across processing variations are uncertain.

The hypothesis is rejected if thermal exposure produces neither significant Mg grain-boundary segregation and a continuous Mg-rich scale nor an increase in localized corrosion relative to the as-cast control.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as having a homogeneous or uniform distribution of all constituent elements while also containing dispersed intermetallic precursor phases; chemically distinct intermetallic phases ordinarily imply at least some elemental partitioning, so the meaning and spatial scale of 'homogeneous' require qualification.
